record.title: Project 2025 Medicaid Caps and Earlier Medicaid/SNAP Block-Grant Proposals
record.description_short: Project 2025 proposed Medicaid block grants or per-capita caps; a separate 2017 NWLC report discussed earlier proposals affecting Medicaid and SNAP.
record.description_medium: Georgetown’s Center for Children and Families reported that Project 2025 would cap federal Medicaid funding through block grants or per-capita limits. NWLC’s 2017 report discussed separate proposals to cap Medicaid and SNAP funding and projected possible effects. Neither supplied source documents a Trump administration conversion of both programs or realized effects.
record.description_long:
Georgetown’s Center for Children and Families described Project 2025 as a policy agenda for a potential second Trump administration and reported that it would convert federal Medicaid funding to block grants or per-capita caps. The article says the plan did not specify how the caps would initially be set or adjusted each year. It explains that fixed federal contributions would no longer track states’ actual costs and discusses risks if enrollment, health-care costs, or unexpected needs grew faster than capped funding. Those effects are projected risks, not reported outcomes.

The National Women’s Law Center’s 2017 report is separate and predates Project 2025. It discusses congressional proposals at that time to cap Medicaid and SNAP funding and analyzes possible effects on eligible people and state budgets. It does not establish that Project 2025 proposed converting SNAP. Neither supplied article documents a 2025 Trump administration conversion of Medicaid or SNAP, eliminated matching payments, required state service cuts, or realized harms.

supports: The article describes Project 2025 as an agenda for a potential second Trump administration.
It says the plan would convert federal Medicaid funding to block grants or per-capita caps.
It says the plan does not specify the caps’ initial amounts or annual adjustments and explains that caps would limit federal contributions regardless of states’ actual costs.
It presents effects from funding caps as projected risks, including failure to keep pace with enrollment, health-care costs, or unexpected needs.
limitations: The article does not document implementation by the Trump administration or realized effects.
It does not establish that Project 2025 proposed converting SNAP to a block grant.

supports: The May 22, 2017 report discusses then-current congressional proposals to cap Medicaid and SNAP funding through block grants and analyzes possible effects on eligible people, benefits, and state budgets.
The report describes possible effects as consequences of proposals, not observed outcomes of a 2025 administration action.
limitations: The report predates Project 2025 and cannot support attributing SNAP block-grant proposals to that blueprint.
It does not document implementation of the described proposals as a 2025 Trump administration action.

source_provenance.focused_rescue: Reviewed the two supplied URLs and narrowed the copy to the proposal and projected-risk claims those sources support; no additional source or event was added.

record.rationale: The focused source review supports Project 2025 Medicaid funding caps as a proposal, plus a distinct 2017 NWLC discussion of Medicaid and SNAP block-grant proposals. Factual correction: removed the original claims that Trump implemented a joint Medicaid/SNAP conversion, eliminated matching payments, forced state service cuts, and caused realized harms. The supplied sources do not support those implementation claims or attributing SNAP conversion to Project 2025. The prior held204 release-ready flag was not treated as approval.
